body: The RAZR’s alarm goes off at twenty to twelve, set at a quarter past four this morning by a man in a blazer who believed in him. He has been lying down for seven and a half hours and asleep for maybe three of them, in pieces. The phone went off on the desk at ten past seven. Theo’s alarm went off at eight and was argued with until twenty past. At nine Theo went out, and the door said so. Now the blind is white with noon at the edges, and the blazer has slept in the shape of him. The visitor pass is still in the breast pocket. It crackles when he turns over. Somewhere behind him in the night there was rain on a stage roof, two and a half hours of the 101, and Doug Pruitt’s wrist, in that order.
He gets the phone open on his chest.

body.text: Thank you. Going in. —L.

body: At twelve past ten she came out the other side of Book Nine:

body.text: Outis. 9.366. Two pages on the pun. I think I passed. Holy day — you going? —L.

body: He leaves her question on the screen and doesn’t answer it yet.

body.text: Holy day. Fitch posted it: 7, 12:10, 5:30. This one isn’t a Thursday. Respectfully, get up. -K

body: Across Ocean Road it has been the Immaculate Conception since midnight. A holy day of obligation: the Church’s word, and the Church picked it on purpose. He works at seven. Between this bed and the Anchor there are two Masses and one pillow, and the pillow is ahead on points.

choices.key: On the Immaculate Conception you got up on three hours’ sleep for the 12:10.
On the Immaculate Conception you slept two more hours and went at 5:30.
On the Immaculate Conception — a holy day of obligation — you slept through it.

body: On a holy day the twelve-ten fills like a Sunday that forgot to dress. Noon comes down through the blue glass onto more people than the weekday pews were built for: graduate students on their lunch hour, two nurses in scrubs with their badges turned around, a man in a FedEx uniform on one knee at the end of a pew, freshmen standing three deep along the back wall under the hull. The altar is in white and so is Father Osei, and somebody has put white roses and a gold ribbon at the foot of the Marian shrine in the side aisle. Gus Ferreira takes the entrance hymn at the organ at the speed of a man bringing a boat in against the tide, and the whole church comes in on the *Ave* like a crew.

Mrs. Fitch has her end of the back pew and her purse on her knees, and is giving the standing room a look that says it might have come in October too. Kevin is in the fourth pew on the right, where he always is, with a Bible at the end of it holding the place. He moves it when Jack genuflects.
“Seat,” Kevin whispers.
He keeps his eyes front. “You never answered the Bible,” he whispers, and opens the missalette to the readings.

The first reading is the garden, after the apple: God calling to the man, *Where are you?*, and the man answering that he heard Him, and was afraid, and hid. Then the Gloria, which comes back for a solemnity even in Advent, and which Gus plays as if he’s been saving it since Thanksgiving. Then Luke, and the angel coming in to a girl in a town in Galilee: *Hail, full of grace! The Lord is with you.*

Father Osei comes down out of the ambo for the homily, which he does when he’s serious, and stands in the aisle at the head of the pews with the bad leg taking a rest. “Luke wrote in Greek,” he says, “and I am going to spend three minutes on one Greek word. Then I will let you go back to your examinations, which is a penance I could not improve on.”

“The angel comes into the house and says, *Chaire, kecharitōmenē.* We say, *Hail, full of grace.* Good. But listen to the shape of the word. It is a perfect participle. A perfect participle is a thing that was done to you, all the way, in the past, and is still true of you now. *Already, and completely, graced.* He does not say, *you will be graced, if.* He does not say, *you are being graced, as you improve.* He says it is done. And he says it where her name should go.”
“He says it before she has said yes to anything. Before she has done one thing worth putting in a homily. That is the scandal of this feast. God gives first.”

“In my first life I was a doctor, and I have held, I suppose, a thousand newborn children. Not one of them had accomplished anything. Every one of them was loved entirely before it had done a single useful thing, and nearly all of them complained about it at the top of their lungs.” The church laughs, the standing room loudest. “Paul uses the same verb in the second reading. The grace He *granted* us in the Beloved — it is the same word. For her it came first, and whole. For us it comes at the font, and then we spend our lives trying to earn what we were handed in the cradle. You cannot earn a gift. You can open it. Or you can leave it on the table with the paper still on, because you are still deciding whether you deserve it.” He looks out at the three deep along the back wall. “Open it.”

At the sign of peace Joey Abruzzo reaches across two pews to pump his hand. “JACK. Holy *day*,” Joey says, at a volume that turns Mrs. Fitch’s head from the back, and goes back to his own pew radiant.
After Communion Jack kneels with his face in his hands and gives Him the list, short, the way it comes: Nonna’s arm. Tariq. Danny. Doug Pruitt’s sleep, whatever Doug Pruitt’s sleep needs.

At the door Osei is shaking hands in his white vestments with the line going out past him into the cold sun. He takes Jack’s hand and keeps it a moment in the doctor’s grip. “Mr. Costigan. On a Tuesday.”
“It’s a holy day, Father.”
“I know,” says Osei. “I was there.”

On the steps Kevin shrugs into his backpack. “Lena’s going tonight,” he says. “The five-thirty, with Julian. She told me after her final.” He points two steps down. “Also, you’re being hunted,” and he’s off toward the library.

Becca is at the bottom of the steps with the clipboard on her hip, and for the length of a sentence she’s shy with him. “Hi. You look like you slept, for once.” After that she’s all clipboard. “You’re on my list.”

body.title: Becca’s clipboard
body.text:
ADVENT PARTY — WHITE ELEPHANT — FRI 7 PM
$10 LIMIT. WRAP IT. NOTHING THAT EATS.
1. Joey (NOT A CRAB)
2. Kevin
3.

body: “Ten dollars,” she says, and taps the line with her pen. “Nothing that eats. Mrs. Fitch says last year somebody brought a ferret and it got into the lemon bars. And Joey asked me if a crab counts.” She looks at Jack, appalled on a crab’s behalf. “A crab *eats*, Joey.”
She writes COSTIGAN on line three in block capitals without asking. “Speaking of. Thomas is going home for Christmas.”
“To Idaho?”

“The lab said yes, if I keep him at thirty-three parts per thousand. I bought the salt mix. He’s riding in a Tupperware with holes in the lid, under the seat in front of me.” She hugs the clipboard. “He’s never seen snow.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow.

response: “Tell Thomas Merry Christmas.”
“I’ll tell him in Idaho,” Becca says. “He’ll be so confused.” She tucks the clipboard under her arm, pleased to the boots, and heads off down Ocean Road toward the Marine Lab to tell him now.

choices.text: “Bring him to the white elephant. He’d go for twelve, easy.”
response: “Bring him to the white elephant. He’d go for twelve, easy.”

“Jack. He’s not a *gift*.” She’s laughing before she gets to the end of it, and writes something in the margin of the clipboard that is probably a note about him, and goes off down Ocean Road toward the lab with the braid swinging.
“Have a good flight, Becca.”
“You too.” She hugs the clipboard. “Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. I looked.”
It’s kindly meant. She’s off down Ocean Road toward the lab before it can land on him, and it lands on him anyway, halfway down the steps.

body: By half past five the blue glass has gone dark and given the church back to the candles. They’re everywhere tonight: on the altar, banked in red cups at the Marian shrine, set along the sills of the black windows, and the ribs of the hull overhead catch the light and hold it like the inside of a lantern. The pews are full of people who came straight from the library with their backpacks still on, and the back wall is standing room. Gus Ferreira is at the organ in a tie. Mrs. Fitch is at the door with a stack of worship aids, and hands Jack one off the top. “Not at the twelve-ten, Mr. Costigan,” she says. She was at the twelve-ten. She is at all of them.

Jack gets the end of a pew on the left, behind a family with a baby asleep in a car seat in the aisle. Two pews ahead of him, on the other side of the aisle, is the black lace mantilla. Julian is beside her in one of his father’s cardigans, the gray one, and when they stand he holds the hymnal open for both of them, low, where she can see it without asking. When they came in he stopped at the end of the pew with one hand on it while she genuflected. He doesn’t genuflect himself. He waits for her to, every time, and goes in after. He has the responses now, all of them, and says them a hair early, like a man proud of a new language.
The first reading is the garden after the apple — *Where are you?* — and the man who heard, and was afraid, and hid. The Gospel is the angel and the girl. *Hail, full of grace.*

Father Osei preaches from the aisle in his evening voice, which is his noon voice with the lights down. He looks the church over first. “I see some faces from the seven o’clock,” he says, “who are very holy, and a great many faces who were asleep at noon, who are very honest.” The honest ones laugh.

The angel’s word is a perfect participle, he says — *kecharitōmenē*, already and completely graced, before she had said yes to anything, before she had done one thing worth a homily. “Some of you sat examinations today,” he says. “You are waiting to be graded. This is the one feast in the year where the Church tells you the grade came first.” A ripple goes along the backpacks. “Do not think she did not need a Savior. She needed Him first. The rest of us He pulls out of the ditch after we have fallen in. Her He caught on the edge, before she fell. It is the same pair of hands. God gives first. Everything else in her life is what she did with a gift she had already opened. Go and do likewise. Then go and sleep.”

At the sign of peace she turns to the pew behind her and sees Jack over it, two rows back. *Peace be with you*, she mouths, and Julian, turning with her, lifts a hand to Jack across the pews, the way you’d wave to somebody across a street.

At Communion Julian stays in the pew and turns his knees to let her out, and she goes up alone and kneels on the hard floor at the front to receive, the lace forward over her face, and comes back with her hands folded. He moves his knees for her again.

The closing hymn is the one every Catholic in America can sing in their sleep. Gus gives it the full foghorn and the church comes in under him: *Immaculate Mary, your praises we sing.* Julian doesn’t know it. He reads the first verse off the page half a bar behind everybody and comes in on the *Ave* late, and wrong. The second time round he has it — *Ave, Ave* — by ear, off no page, right on it, the easy baritone Jack has heard at Bastille under her alto.
Lena doesn’t turn her head. The lace moves a little at her temple, and she sings the next one louder.
On the last *Ave* the RAZR goes off in his jacket, against his ribs: the double buzz of a picture message.
Two pews ahead, Lena doesn’t turn around.

choices.text: Put your hand over it and keep singing.
response: He covers the pocket with his hand and keeps singing, a verse he’s known since second grade, until the thing under his hand goes still.
Outside it’s twenty past six and full dark, the steps lit by the open doors. Down on Ocean Road the 6:20 is pulling away from the stop with its windows yellow, and he’s due at the Anchor at seven.

Lena comes out between Julian and the door with the mantilla already off and folded into her missal. She finds Jack on the steps. “*Kecharitōmenē*,” she says, as though they’ve been in the middle of it all day. “He got the perfect participle *right*, Youngstown. I could have kissed Father Osei —” and she hears it a word too late, and laughs it into Julian’s shoulder, her forehead against the gray cardigan.
Julian, who doesn’t have the Greek, looks pleased anyway, and holds the door for the family with the car seat.

choices.text: Switch it off inside your pocket.
response: He finds the power key by feel through the lining and holds it down. The phone plays its little falling chime on the way out, clear as a bell in the gap after the *Ave*, and a woman in the pew in front of him turns around in the pew to look.

body: He wakes in the dark and doesn’t know which dark. The blind is black. The desk lamp on Theo’s side is on and Theo isn’t, and the clock on the outer screen of the RAZR says 6:20, and it takes him a long, thick-headed minute to work out that it’s the evening of the same day.
The five-thirty is at Communion by now. The twelve-ten was six hours ago. The Anchor is in forty minutes.
It’s the first holy day of obligation he has missed since he was sixteen. He sits on the edge of the bed in the blazer with his socks on the cold floor and doesn’t argue with it.

Through the slats of the blind, across Ocean Road and the dark of the Grove, the blue glass of St. Brendan’s is lit from inside. From up here, at night, it sits in the trees like a ship with its lights on, which is what the architect wanted. He says an Act of Contrition on the edge of the bed, fast, like a man apologizing on his way into a room he’s late for, and gets up. The Old Mission will have an evening Mass. He doesn’t know when, and the Anchor is at seven, and Gloria is short a dishwasher on a Tuesday.
Under the clock on the outer screen there is a little envelope, and 6:18. Inside, under it, there’s Kevin:

body.text: The Bible waited till the Gospel. Then it gave your seat to a nurse. -K

body: He’ll owe it on Saturday, behind the screen, in a converted coat closet, to a man who used to be a doctor.

He gets out of the blazer and into the work shirt, and finds the apron on the back of the chair, and the second boot under Theo’s bed. At 6:41, at the door, with his coat half on, the phone goes again.

body.text: Didn’t see you at the 5:30. Kevin says not at the 12:10 either. Osei said “full of grace” means she was already graced before she’d done a single thing. Kecharitomene. Perfect participle. I thought you’d want it. —L.

body: He stands in the open door with the hall light on his boots and her text in his hand, and the envelope still sitting under it, unopened.

choices.text: *overslept. i owe a confession. thank you for the participle*

response.text: overslept. i owe a confession. thank you for the participle
Saturday 3:30. I’ll save you a place in line. —L.

response: He reads it going down the east stairs, and it carries him most of the way to the bus.
It comes in while he’s on the stairs, the whole of it, and weighs about what it should.
He shuts the phone on both of them, the envelope and the participle, and puts it in the apron pocket, and pulls 412’s door to behind him.

body: He got in off Mission Street a little after two with the phone still warm in his hand and slept like a dropped coat, and at twenty past eight he’s going down the fourth-floor hall in yesterday’s Carhartt with his toothbrush, past the east-stair door and the EXIT sign and the red handle under it, which he gives a long look.

body.text: The fourth-floor lounge at twenty past eight is the microwave counting down somebody’s oatmeal and the squeak of a dry-erase marker. Margot is at the whiteboard in black, with a coffee already going cold on the sill beside her. She has taken UNEXPLAINED CITRUS off the top of the board with the side of her fist — a gray smear is all that’s left of it — and left Laney’s pink column alone. In its place, in her capitals:

body.title: 4th-floor lounge whiteboard
body.text:
FIRE ALARMS (5): CASE CLOSED.
SUSPECT: PRUITT, D. (ASLEEP).
WITNESS: COSTIGAN, J. (UNEXPLAINED).

TIGER — A COUNT (L.P.): MORE.

Doug Pruitt comes in for cereal in the hoodie and his green Crocs and stops dead in front of the board with the box of Lucky Charms against his chest. He reads it with his lips moving, top to bottom, and back up to his own name.
“Dude,” he says. “Am I *famous*?”
“You’re a *sleepwalker*, Douglas,” says Margot.
Doug considers this with everything he has. “…*Rad*.”

“October the thirteenth,” Margot tells him, “you came out of the wrong fire door in what was left of a typhoon and walked through a puddle to the ankle without breaking stride. I had you down as *indifferent to weather*.” She looks at the board. “I was wrong about the adjective.”
“Does that mean I did all *five*?”

“It means you’re asleep at four in the morning with your eyes open, Douglas, during finals.” She hands him back the Lucky Charms, which he has set down beside her coffee. “Eat something. Go to bed at a Christian hour.”

Kevin comes in behind Jack with his mug, reads the board over the top of it, and says, “Huh. Parasomnia. That tracks,” and looks at Doug with real medical tenderness, and at the WITNESS line, and at Jack, and goes to fill the mug.
Margot caps the marker and turns around and looks at Jack in the doorway with his toothbrush. “The witness,” she says, “may wish to make a statement.”

Every time the door of 420 moves, it jingles. Kevin has hung a Christmas bell on the inside knob on a loop of dental floss — mint, waxed — and inside, in the hoodie, Doug is asking the room in general why the door is festive.

Kevin is in the doorway in the navy quarter-zip with the orgo text under his arm, on his way out, and he has already done all of it. “Priya at seven,” he tells Jack. “In her doorway, in her retainer. The health center gets a call the Monday after finals. The bell stays.”
“Because you’re a flight risk,” Kevin says over his shoulder. “Non-REM parasomnia. Textbook. Stress plus sleep debt, and it’s finals.”
From inside: “Is that *bad*?”
“It’s festive,” says Kevin.

Doug comes to the door in the hoodie, setting off the bell, with his hair flat on one side. “Dude,” he says to Jack, warmly. “I don’t remember *any* of it. Kevin says you were *there*.” He shakes Jack’s hand, toothbrush and all. “Thanks, dude.” He goes back in to his cereal, jingling.
“The raid boss is nine feet tall,” Kevin says. “I got a full description at breakfast. He doesn’t remember telling me.”
Then Kevin looks at Jack straight. Not at the blazer, which is on a hanger, or the pass, which is in a drawer. At Jack. “Why were *you* in the hall at four, Jack?”
“On the lawn Saturday I erased a question mark next to your name,” Kevin says. “I’m drawing it back in.”
In Jack’s pocket the RAZR buzzes, and his hand is on it before the second buzz. Kevin’s eyes go to the pocket, and come back up.

The fourth-floor lounge at twenty past eight is Priya’s laminator, warming up on the table and complaining about it. She is making NO SHOES IN HALLWAYS (FIRE CODE) again, a size larger, for the lounge. UNEXPLAINED CITRUS — FLOORS 2–4 is still at the top of Margot’s whiteboard, with THE CATHOLICS still listed under it as the suspects.

body.title: Priya’s new laminate, the lounge door
body.text:
NO SHOES IN HALLWAYS (FIRE CODE)
THIS INCLUDES THE LOUNGE.
THIS INCLUDES CROCS.
— Priya, RA, 401
Doug Pruitt is at the counter under the window in the hoodie, eating Lucky Charms out of the box with his fingers. He’s barefoot. There is grass on the soles of his feet.

“Dude,” Doug says, when he sees Jack. “I had the *craziest* dream. You were in it.” He eats a marshmallow horseshoe. “You had a *jacket* on. And there was a raid boss in the elevator, and you were all, like, *I’ll tell him*.” He points a horseshoe at Jack. “Did you tell him?”

The laminator takes a sheet in and thinks about it. Priya looks up from it at Doug’s feet, and at the grass on them, and opens her mouth, and closes it, and feeds the laminator another sheet. “Five alarms, Costigan,” she tells Jack instead. “The fire marshal knows my first name. He uses it.”
Doug looks at Jack, puzzled and friendly. “Why’d you have a jacket on?”

choices.text: “I was up with a sick friend.”
response: “I was up with a sick friend.”

response.text: “Douglas *is* the sick friend,” says Margot, and picks up her cold coffee, and drinks it anyway.
“Your friends get sick at noon,” Kevin says. “I’ve met them.” He goes off down the hall with the orgo book, and behind him 420’s door jingles shut.
Doug thinks about it. His face falls. “Dude,” he says. “Was it *me*?”

response: “I was out.”

response.text: “I know,” says Margot. She leaves the WITNESS line up.
“I know you were out,” Kevin says. He pulls the door to, and the bell jingles behind it, and he goes to class.
Doug nods slowly, a man in the presence of mystery. “…Rad.”
Margot looks at him over the capped marker. Then she leaves the line up and takes her coffee to class.
Kevin waits about as long as a polite man waits for an answer, and then he goes to class.
Doug doesn’t notice. He’s already explaining the raid boss to Priya, who has stopped laminating to listen with an expression of growing professional concern.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Tuesday at four in the morning she opened 305 before I knocked. Wednesday: FIRE ALARMS (5): CASE CLOSED. SUSPECT: PRUITT, D. (ASLEEP). WITNESS: COSTIGAN, J. (UNEXPLAINED).

body: The last seminar gets the best light of the semester: low winter sun straight down the long table from the west windows, so bright on the wood that half the table sits squinting like card players. Yusuf’s chair is the third one down on the window side, empty. Caleb has learned.

Hale comes in at one o’clock exactly, which has never happened, in a dark jacket Jack hasn’t seen before, pressed, with nothing on either cuff. He sits down. “Mr. Noorzai flies back tonight,” he says. “His chair has been very patient. Let us be the same.”

He spends the last hour where he spent the first one, in September — *prove to me you have a soul* — only this time he argues for it himself and makes them take it apart, and when Caleb takes it apart with Hume, Hale tells him that was very nearly a sentence.

Lena says nothing. She sits across from Jack with her pen capped and her notebook shut and the sun on her hands, and listens, and for an hour she doesn’t open her mouth: not to Caleb, not to Hale, not when Hale walks right up to the edge of an argument she has been winning since September and stands there waiting for her.
At two o’clock Hale looks at the clock, and then down the table. “Miss Broussard has said nothing for an hour,” he says mildly. “Note the date.”
“I’m saving it for Wednesday, Professor.”

She smiles when she says it. Her face is very bright, and looks washed, recently and hard, in cold water: the face of somebody who has been handed something too big to carry home. She meets Jack’s eyes across the table, and uncaps her pen, and caps it again.
“Wednesday the sixteenth,” Hale says. “Two at a time, each of you defending the other’s best argument, with me in the way. You know that much. Here is what you don’t know.”

“By Friday each of you will email me which argument of the other’s you intend to defend. Choose the best one. If you choose a weak one in order to win, I shall know.” He looks down the table at the pairs. “So will they.”

He picks up his coffee. “Tomorrow the President accepts a prize for peace, nine days after sending thirty thousand more young men to a war. He will have to say something clever about that, and he will. Read it. One of you will want to quote it at me next Wednesday.” He drinks. “Resist.”
At the door, getting into his coat, he says to the hall: “I shall have the town to myself again in a week.”

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know.

s14a.slug: THURSDAY · 4:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: CNN has been running Oslo since four in the morning, and at half past four in the afternoon it’s still on the Fishbowl’s TV with the sound down to one bar: the President at a lectern in a hall full of Norwegians in evening clothes, giving the same speech again to a lounge that is mostly studying. Outside the glass the Lagoon has gone gold. Margot has the armchair and the transcript, printed off the White House website in the library at seven this morning and already red in the margins. Lena is on the couch with her knees up and a Greek lexicon she no longer needs open on them, out of habit.

Yusuf is back. He flew in last night, and he’s at the end of the couch where he sat for West Point, with one hand on the arm beside him, holding it. When Jack comes in he takes the hand away. “My mother says thank you,” he says, low, when Jack sits. “For the stairs. The other stairs.” That’s all he says about it.

Margot reads off the transcript without any expression at all. “‘Evil does exist in the world. A non-violent movement could not have halted Hitler’s armies. Negotiations cannot convince al Qaeda’s leaders to lay down their arms.’” She looks up. “Costigan.”
“I agree with every word,” Jack says, and hears himself. “I agree with every word a Democrat said in Norway. I’m going to have to call my father, and neither one of us is going to know what to say.”
“‘I face the world as it is,’” Margot reads. She lowers the page. “He accepted a *peace* prize for a *surge*.”
“He gave the conditions himself,” Lena says from the couch. “Last resort. Proportion. Spare the civilians. Augustine would grade it a B and ask him to name the week in eight years we met all three.”
“You can’t grade a war by the week.”
“Watch me, Costigan.”
“Dorothy Day would’ve sent the prize money to the Catholic Worker,” she says, “and the medal back to Oslo. Postage due.”

Laney puts her head in at the Fishbowl door with her hair up in a towel. “Lena. Seven-thirty. I am doing your hair whether you want it done or not.” She sees the TV. “Is he *still* talking?” And she’s gone.
Yusuf has been watching the President with his hands between his knees. “My brother’s learning stairs,” he says. “I’d like the speech to be right.”
On the screen the President goes on, a bar too low to hear. Margot lets the transcript down onto her knee.

choices.text: Agree with the President out loud.
response: “He’s right,” Jack says, to the room, and to Yusuf. “There’s evil in the world, and some people go and stand between it and everybody else. You can hate that it’s true. It’s still true.”
Lena looks at him over her knees. “Write the date down, Margot.”
“I’m not giving you the satisfaction of ink,” says Margot.
“The stairs,” Jack says. “What are they like?”

Yusuf tells him. Parallel bars first, in a long room with a mirror at the end of it so you can watch yourself do it wrong. Then a walker, which Tariq hates and has named. Then the stairs: eleven of them, a rail on each side, a therapist one step below him the whole way. “Monday he did all eleven,” Yusuf says. “My mother counted them on the phone, out loud, to my father, who was standing right there.” He almost smiles. “My father said he could count.”

choices.text: “I need Margot to tell me I’m wrong so I can feel normal.”
response: “I need Margot to tell me I’m wrong so I can feel normal.”
“You’re wrong,” says Margot, turning a page.
“Thank you,” says Jack. “I feel much better.”

journal.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us. Broke the fast with his people on Mission Street and fed me till I couldn’t stand. Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks. His nineteenth, at Bastille, with a candle in a scone. He watched the memorial Tuesday. Standing up. I didn’t ask. The night of the West Point speech: ‘You left the first time. My father watched you leave. If you’re going to come, stay.’ His brother Tariq — an IED in Helmand. Alive. Germany. I went after him. We sat on the east stairs. Back for finals the night before Oslo. Tariq’s learning stairs. He’d like the speech to be right.
